## Overview

The Tolowa, also called *Taa-laa-wa Dee-niʼ*, are an Athabaskan nation of Native Americans whose traditional homeland, *Taa-laa-waa-dvn*, lies along the Pacific Coast between Wilson Creek and the Smith River basin in Del Norte in northwestern California. Their territory extends from the California–Oregon border to Wilson Creek, north of the Klamath River. They lived in approximately eight permanent villages around present-day Crescent City Harbor and Lake Earl, including Yontocket, their most important village. Two rancherías, Smith River and Elk Valley, remain in their traditional territory, while others were removed to the Siletz Reservation in Oregon. Population estimates vary: the sources report 1,000 Tolowa in 1770, 150 in 1910, and approximately 1,000 in 2009. Their language belongs to the Pacific Coast subgroup of the Athabaskan language family.

## Material culture

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do document boats, which allowed the Tolowa to travel into the ocean to hunt seals, sea lions, and sea otters.

## Music & performance

They do describe communal gatherings at Yontocket, where people from surrounding areas assembled for celebrations and discussions. The Tolowa embraced the Ghost Dance religion from 1872 to 1882 in hopes of obtaining relief from European-American encroachment.

The sources also mention Marr / Harrington sound recordings of Tolowa and the Siletz Talking Dictionary as documentation resources. Alfred “Bud” Lane recorded 14,000 words of Siletz Dee-ni in an online audio/picture dictionary, and the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians produced a “talking dictionary” in 2007 in coordination with the Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages.

## Dance & theatre

## Festivals & rituals

The sources identify Needash celebrations as important communal occasions. Tolowa people were repeatedly attacked while gathered at these celebrations, and the Yontoket Massacre devastated Yontocket, which had been a cultural center where people from surrounding areas gathered for celebrations and discussions.

The Tolowa embraced the Ghost Dance religion from 1872 to 1882. The sources explain that this occurred in response to European-American encroachment.

## Foodways

Tolowa subsistence centered on riverine and marine resources and acorns, called *san-chvn*. The ocean and rivers supplied lamprey eels, large ocean mussels, smelt, seals, sea lions, sea otters, and whales that washed ashore. Smelt were caught, dried on the beach, and preserved for later consumption. Acorns were a vital food source, supplemented by nuts, berries, and seeds.

The Tolowa used boats to travel into the ocean to hunt seals, sea lions, and sea otters on offshore rocks. Whales that washed ashore were claimed by the nearest village.

## Oral tradition & literature

They do describe Yontocket as a place where surrounding communities gathered for celebrations and discussions, and they mention Tolowa traditional narratives as a related subject.

Contemporary language preservation is documented through the work of Loren Bommelyn, a fluent speaker and linguist who has published pedagogical books and teaches young Tolowa students in Crescent City, California. The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians produced a “talking dictionary” in 2007 with the Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages. Alfred “Bud” Lane recorded 14,000 words of Siletz Dee-ni for preservation, teaching, and community use.

## Language & religion

Tolowa has traditionally been called *Taa-laa-wa Dee-niʼ Wee-yaʼ*. It is a member of the Pacific Coast subgroup of the Athabaskan language family. Together with Lower Rogue River Athabaskan, Upper Rogue River Athabaskan or Galice-Applegate, and Upper Umpqua or Etnemitane, it forms an Oregon Athabaskan cluster. At first European contact, Tolowa was spoken in village communities along the Del Norte County coast and the southern coast of adjacent Curry County, Oregon.

Siletz Dee-niʼ is a form of Tolowa historically spoken by members of the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians on the Siletz Indian Reservation in Oregon. In the early 21st century, it was described as the remaining native language spoken at the reservation, although the sources state that it has since been at least partially revived. Tolowa has contrasting aspirated, unaspirated, and ejective stops, contrasting vowel length and nasality, and a pitch accent rather than a fully tonal system. Three alphabets have been used since the Tolowa Dee-niʼ Language program began in 1969; a Practical Alphabet was devised in 1993, and Loren Bommelyn developed another alphabet in 1997. They document the Tolowa adoption of the Ghost Dance religion from 1872 to 1882.
